claims.text: The anomalous stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior of HfNbTaTiZr originates from internal residual stresses.
The internal residual stresses are produced by thermal-expansion mismatch among constituent clusters in HfNbTaTiZr.
Thermal-expansion mismatch promotes dynamic strain aging.
Dynamic strain aging and defect pinning govern the alloy's creep behavior.
Dynamic strain aging and defect pinning govern the temperature-dependent elastic moduli.
Dynamic strain aging and defect pinning govern deformation- and aging-induced hardening.
At elevated temperatures, modest thermal-expansion differences among local elemental clusters generate residual stresses.
The mismatch-induced residual stresses impede dislocation mobility.
A minor alloying modification can bring the thermal-expansion coefficients of constituent clusters closer together.
Reducing thermal-expansion mismatch will lower residual-stress levels.
Reducing thermal-expansion mismatch will reduce the tensile creep rate at high temperature.
Reducing thermal-expansion mismatch will produce a more uniform temperature dependence of elastic moduli.
Reducing thermal-expansion mismatch will make aging-induced hardening less pronounced.
The conventional alloy exhibits high-temperature creep, elastic-modulus anomalies, and aging-induced hardening.
The proposed residual-stress mechanism is dominant from approximately 600 to 1250 °C.
Other mechanisms may govern the behavior outside the approximately 600–1250 °C interval.
Short-range ordering may also contribute to the observed behavior.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says mismatch-induced residual stresses impede dislocation mobility, which would ordinarily resist creep, but the prediction says reducing those stresses will also reduce the creep rate. The causal sign of the creep prediction is therefore inconsistent unless an additional rate-accelerating pathway is specified.
